passage:
Week one, the survey team from the agricultural college sat in the village panchayat hall, smiling politely. Everyone said, “Sure, whatever you think,” and nobody argued. Week two, at the tea stall, the arguments began: whose questionnaire to use, who would carry the recorder, why Yusuf had chosen the far hamlets. Rehana felt her stomach knot. She wondered whether to ask to change groups. Yusuf snapped, “I'm not doing the whole thing alone.” Silence.

That evening Rehana sat on the hostel steps and remembered what their professor had said: early friction is normal. Over the next days the team wrote each person's job on the wall, and Yusuf laughed at his own bad handwriting. By week four they were finishing each other's sentences.

qa.q: Where did the survey team sit in week one?
qa.a: The survey team sat in the village panchayat hall, smiling politely.

qa.q: Why did Rehana wonder whether to ask to change groups?
qa.a: Rehana felt anxious about the tension and thought it might mean the team was failing, though early friction is common.

qa.q: What did the team do that helped it settle?
qa.a: The team wrote each person's job on the wall, so roles and expectations were clear.

qa.q: What might Yusuf have felt when snapping, “I'm not doing the whole thing alone”?
qa.a: Yusuf probably felt overloaded and unappreciated, worried about carrying too much.

grounding: A student sees a new project team go from polite to tense to workable and understands that early friction is normal.

passage:
In a seminar room in Prague, Olga's new project team of four met for the first time. Everyone was very polite. “Whatever suits you.” “No, you decide.” Nothing got decided. By the second meeting Leila said, “We keep pretending to agree. Marek's design won't work.” Marek stiffened. Stefan started drumming his fingers. The meeting ended ten minutes early with nobody looking at each other.

Olga walked home thinking they had chosen badly. But her flatmate, who had done group work before, only shrugged. “It's usually like this in week two.” At the third meeting Marek brought a revised design and Leila offered to test it. They split tasks on a shared sheet and finished by nine. Olga noticed she was hungry, and laughing.

qa.q: Where did Olga's team meet for the first time?
qa.a: Olga's team met in a seminar room in Prague.

qa.q: Why did Olga think they had chosen badly?
qa.a: Olga felt discouraged and worried after the tense meeting, reading the tension that followed the polite start as a sign the team was failing.

qa.q: What did Marek and Leila do at the third meeting?
qa.a: Marek brought a revised design and Leila offered to test it.

qa.q: How might Marek have felt when Leila said the design would not work?
qa.a: Marek probably felt stung and defensive at first, which explains stiffening, but later was willing to revise.

grounding: A student sees a new project team go from polite to tense to workable, and understands that early friction is normal.

passage:
In the college microbiology lab, Deepak watched the new project team of five come together.
Week one was all smiles. Everyone said “great idea” to everything. Chetan offered to do the extra readings. Nobody disagreed about anything.
Week three, the smiles disappeared. Chetan and Priyanka argued over the sampling method. Two people stopped coming to meetings. Deepak thought about asking the professor to move him to another team.
Their teaching assistant said, “This is normal. Teams fight before they settle. Just don't quit now.”
Week six, they made a simple rule: disagree in meetings, not in the corridor. Chetan did the sampling, Priyanka did the analysis. The arguments got shorter.
Deepak was glad he'd stayed.

qa.q: Which week did the smiles disappear?
qa.a: Week three.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel in week three?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and discouraged, thinking about asking to move to another team.

qa.q: What helped the team move from tense to workable?
qa.a: Knowing early fights are normal, making a rule to disagree in meetings, and dividing work by strengths.

qa.q: How might Chetan have felt during the week-three arguments?
qa.a: Chetan was probably frustrated and defensive about the sampling method.

grounding: Shows a student watching a new project team move from polite to tense to workable, and learning early friction is normal.

passage:
Dear Leela di,
You asked how my research team is going. Honestly, I nearly wrote to you last month to say I was quitting.
The first two weeks were lovely. Everyone agreed with everyone. I thought, this will be easy.
Then it fell apart. Rohan wanted to change the topic. Meera said Rohan never listened. I spent evenings dreading group meetings. I actually drafted a message to our professor asking to work alone.
I remembered you saying teams always go through a bad patch before they work. So I didn't send it.
This week we finally divided the work properly, and yesterday's meeting was the best one yet. Still some arguments, but useful ones.
Thank you for that advice.
Anirban

qa.q: What did Anirban draft a message to the professor about?
qa.a: Asking to work alone.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel during the bad patch?
qa.a: Anirban felt anxious and discouraged, dreading group meetings and nearly quitting.

qa.q: What kept Anirban from giving up, and why was it helpful?
qa.a: Remembering Leela di's advice that teams go through a bad patch, which helped Anirban stay until the team settled.

qa.q: How might Leela di feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Leela di would likely feel pleased and proud that the advice helped.

grounding: A student writes about a new research team going from polite to tense to workable, and nearly quitting before understanding friction is normal.

passage:
So, first-year engineering project? I'm Asif, and I nearly quit.
Our team of four met in September. For two weeks we were so polite. “Sure, whatever you think.” Sharmila, me, two others. Nobody said what they actually wanted.
Then October hit. Sharmila and Varun had a big fight about the design. I stopped wanting to go to meetings. I remember sitting on the hostel steps thinking, I'll just tell the professor I'll do it alone.
But my senior said, “Every team fights in the middle. If you leave now, you'll never see it settle.”
So I stayed. By November, we'd sorted roles, and the fights were quicker. The bridge model came second in the department. Now I tell every first-year: wait for the settling.

qa.q: What did the model come in the department?
qa.a: The bridge model came second in the department.

qa.q: How did Asif feel sitting on the hostel steps?
qa.a: Asif felt discouraged and fed up, thinking about quitting to work alone.

qa.q: What advice kept Asif in the team, and why was it wise?
qa.a: The senior said every team fights in the middle and that leaving too early means never seeing it settle, which gave Asif patience.

qa.q: How might Sharmila have felt during the October fight?
qa.a: Sharmila was probably frustrated and tense, arguing hard about the design.

grounding: A student recalls a new project team going from polite to tense to workable, and nearly quitting before seeing friction is normal.

passage:
I'm Tarun, and I was the quietest one in our five-member design project team, so mostly I watched.
Week one, everyone was polite. Mehak said "great idea" to everything. Nobody disagreed, and we got almost nothing done.
Week three, it cracked. Mehak and Arjun argued for twenty minutes about the colour scheme, then about who was "always late". Pooja walked out once. I sat there with my stomach churning and seriously thought about asking to switch teams.
Week five, something shifted. Mehak said, "I'll take layout, Arjun takes colour, and we stop fighting about each other's parts." Arjun actually laughed. We started meeting on time.
I can't say what changed in their heads. But I'm glad I didn't leave in week three, because the team we became was better than the polite one.

qa.q: How long did Mehak and Arjun argue about the colour scheme?
qa.a: For twenty minutes.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel during week three?
qa.a: Tarun felt anxious, stomach churning, and was tempted to switch teams.

qa.q: What might Tarun tell another quiet member stuck in a week-three team?
qa.a: That early fights are normal, and teams often find a way to split the work if you stay and give it time.

qa.q: How might Mehak have experienced the change from week three to week five?
qa.a: Mehak probably felt frustrated during the fights, then relieved to find a split that let everyone own a part.

grounding: Shows a student watching a new project team move from polite to tense to workable, and staying instead of giving up.
